The Giant cichlid Boulengerochromis microlepis is one of the largest cichlid species in the world, with adults attaining a maximum recorded body mass of 7 kilograms [Wwi = 7 kilograms]. This impressive ultimate size is matched by equally striking dimensions in length; field surveys and angling records indicate that the species reaches an ultimate total length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters], making it a dominant piscivore within its endemic Lake Tanganyikan habitat. At the opposite end of the life cycle, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size. Based on the typical egg diameter observed in related tilapiine cichlids such as Oreochromis niloticus, the estimated wet weight at birth for Boulengerochromis microlepis is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a value that underscores the extreme ontogenetic trajectory this species must complete to reach its seven-kilogram adult form. This dramatic increase in mass from the larval stage to the fully grown adult represents one of the most pronounced size transformations documented among African cichlids and is closely tied to its prolonged growing period and high trophic position within the lake ecosystem.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a body size considerably smaller than the ultimate maximum, marking a clear separation between the onset of reproductive capacity and continued somatic growth. Wild-caught individuals examined during reproductive surveys typically attain puberty at a total length of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 891 grams [Wwp = approximately 891 grams]. This value was derived from length-weight regressions applied to field specimens, following the relationship established from the species' growth curve. The transition to reproductive maturity at this size implies that individuals invest a substantial portion of their early life in reaching a body mass sufficient to support the energetic demands of nest construction, egg production, and the intensive biparental care for which this species is renowned. The considerable gap between the weight at puberty, just under one kilogram, and the ultimate mass of seven kilograms indicates that post-maturational growth continues for many years, allowing reproductively active adults to gradually increase in size throughout their long lives.

At a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a condition that closely matches the thermal regime of the shallow littoral zones where this species breeds, Boulengerochromis microlepis exhibits a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 10,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 10,000 eggs per year], a strategy that aligns with the species' role as a long-lived, iteroparous predator investing heavily in the protection of each brood. The repeated spawning cycles are facilitated by the stable, warm temperatures of the lake environment, which sustain high metabolic rates and rapid gonadal recrudescence between brooding intervals.

Longevity records for Boulengerochromis microlepis indicate that this species is one of the longest-lived cichlids known, with a lifespan that extends considerably beyond that of most other members of the Cichlidae family. Under natural conditions in Lake Tanganyika, where the water temperature remains consistently around 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum documented lifespan is approximately 5,475 days [am = approximately 5,475 days], which translates to roughly 15 years. This extraordinary longevity is remarkable for a teleost of its size and is thought to be linked to the species' slow pace of life, its position as a top predator within a stable, ancient lake ecosystem, and the intensive parental care that reduces juvenile mortality and selects for a longer reproductive window. The extended lifespan allows individuals to accumulate body mass steadily over many years, gradually ascending to the apex of the size distribution within their population and likely conferring a reproductive advantage through increased fecundity and territorial dominance in later life stages.

The reproductive strategy of Boulengerochromis microlepis reflects its position as an apex predator within the Lake Tanganyikan fish community. The species produces approximately 30 to 35 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 30 to 35 eggs per spawning event] and spawns up to 3 times per year [F_R_i = up to 3 times per year], yielding an annual fecundity of roughly 90 to 105 eggs per year. This reproductive output, combined with the large adult body size reaching up to 7,000 grams [Wwi = up to 7,000 grams], places this cichlid among the most size-dimorphic and reproductively conservative members of the family Cichlidae. The growth trajectory from a larval wet weight of just 1.8 milligrams [Wwb = 1.8 milligrams] to an adult body mass that can exceed 7 kilograms represents an increase of over six orders of magnitude, a developmental feat requiring decades of continuous feeding and efficient exploitation of the lake's abundant fish prey. Reaching a length of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters] marks the onset of sexual maturation, while the maximum total length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters] is attained only by the oldest individuals that have survived the cumulative pressures of predation and intraspecific competition over their exceptionally long lives.
